**The Weight of a Single Thought**

The first time I realized the weight of a single thought, I was standing in the middle of a crowded subway station. The air was thick with the hum of voices, the clatter of footsteps, the distant screech of brakes. My mind was a storm—thoughts crashing into each other like waves against a cliff. But one thought, small and quiet, rose above the noise: *What if I just stop moving?*

It wasn’t a suicidal thought, not exactly. It was more like a question, a curiosity. What would happen if I simply stood still, let the world flow around me, and refused to take another step? The idea was so heavy it pressed against my ribs, making it hard to breathe.

I didn’t stop. I kept walking, kept following the current of bodies toward the train. But that thought lingered, settling into the back of my mind like a stone in a shoe. It wasn’t the first time I’d had it, and I knew it wouldn’t be the last.

---

Thoughts are strange things. They don’t weigh anything, not in the physical sense. But they can feel heavier than lead, dragging you down until even the simplest actions—getting out of bed, brushing your teeth, smiling at a stranger—become monumental tasks.

I’ve had thoughts that felt like anchors, pulling me under. Thoughts that twisted my stomach into knots, that made my hands shake, that left me staring at the ceiling at 3 a.m., wondering how I’d ever untangle myself from the mess in my head.

But I’ve also had thoughts that felt like wings. Light, buoyant, lifting me up until I could almost believe I was floating. Thoughts that made me laugh out loud in the middle of the street, that made my heart race with excitement, that made me want to run, to dance, to scream at the top of my lungs.

The problem is, the heavy thoughts are the ones that stick. They’re the ones that replay on a loop, the ones that whisper in the dark when you’re trying to sleep. The light thoughts? They flicker and fade, like fireflies in the night.

---

I used to think that if I could just *stop* thinking, everything would be easier. If I could silence the noise in my head, I’d finally find peace. But the more I tried to push the thoughts away, the louder they became. It was like trying to hold water in my hands—no matter how tightly I clenched my fingers, it slipped through.

Then I learned that thoughts aren’t enemies to be fought. They’re just sounds in the symphony of the mind. Some are discordant, some are harmonious, but all of them are part of the music.

The key isn’t to stop thinking. It’s to *notice* the thoughts. To observe them without judgment, to let them come and go like clouds passing through the sky. Some will linger, some will drift away. But none of them have to define you.

---

I still have heavy thoughts. Some days, they’re so heavy I can barely move. But I’ve learned to carry them differently now. I don’t fight them. I don’t let them swallow me whole. I just… let them be.

And sometimes, when the weight feels unbearable, I remind myself of the light thoughts. The ones that make me feel alive. The ones that remind me that even in the darkest moments, there’s always a flicker of light somewhere.

Because thoughts are just thoughts. They don’t have to control you. You can choose which ones to hold onto, and which ones to let go.

And that’s the real weight of a single thought—it’s not how heavy it is, but how much power you give it.

---

The subway station is still crowded. The air is still thick with noise. But now, when I stand in the middle of it all, I don’t feel the weight of my thoughts pressing down on me. I just feel the rhythm of the world around me, and the quiet hum of my own mind, carrying on.

And that’s enough.
